claims.text: Brittle behavior in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy can emerge following nanoscale grain-boundary segregation.
Grain-boundary segregation produces a local loss of chemical complexity.
The local loss of chemical complexity fosters brittle intermetallic or amorphous phases at grain boundaries.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy.
Intermediate-temperature aging can promote modest grain-boundary segregation while retaining the alloy's overall composition.
Diffusion becomes sufficiently active under an appropriate combination of aging temperature and time to induce selective grain-boundary segregation.
Low-temperature service conditions make brittle failure more likely in the proposed segregated alloy.
Local enrichment of selected constituent elements at grain boundaries diminishes local entropy stabilization.
Diminished local entropy stabilization provokes nanoscale formation of a brittle secondary phase.
Thermal exposure induces limited diffusion and selective grain-boundary segregation.
Segregation-induced local composition changes trigger nucleation of brittle intermetallic or amorphous grain-boundary phases.
The grain-boundary phases lower grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes premature crack initiation and propagation under stress.
Thermally aged specimens will have lower impact toughness than the untreated baseline.
Thermally aged specimens will have lower tensile ductility than the untreated baseline.
Thermally aged specimens will exhibit increased intergranular cracking relative to the untreated baseline.
TEM or atom-probe tomography will reveal nanoscale secondary phases at grain boundaries in aged specimens.
The proposed embrittlement effect is expected primarily under low-temperature or high-strain-rate loading.
Bulk phase separation must be avoided for the comparison to remain within the intended high-entropy-alloy regime.
